name: OpenBLAS
baseline: Netlib reference BLAS (Debian blas 1.2.20110419, single-threaded) and ATLAS 3.10.2 (Debian package, single-threaded); Intel MKL, GotoBLAS2, BLIS and multi-threaded ATLAS dev were measured in the same runs
workload: Wall-clock time of dense linear algebra inside R 3.2.4 (Microsoft R Open) linked to each BLAS on a Xeon E3-1275 v5: R-benchmark-25 style 2800x2800 cross-product and 3000x3000 linear regression (10 runs each), and the gcbd matrix-multiply benchmark up to 5000x5000.
claimed_speedup: OpenBLAS 0.2.12 (multi-threaded Debian package) against single-threaded Netlib reference BLAS and single-threaded ATLAS 3.10.2, medians of the per-run times stored in the repo (derived from page data; the README shows them only as bar charts): 2800x2800 cross-product 0.488 s vs 11.41 s Netlib (about 23x) and 1.50 s ATLAS (about 3.1x); 3000x3000 linear regression 0.261 s vs 5.47 s Netlib (about 21x) and 0.747 s ATLAS (about 2.9x); gcbd 5000x5000 matrix multiply 2.74 s vs 64.9 s Netlib (about 24x) and 8.33 s ATLAS (about 3.0x). Not the fastest in the same charts: Intel MKL needs 0.136 s and multi-threaded ATLAS dev 0.144 s on the cross-product.
hardware: Intel Xeon E3-1275 v5 (host 'term2'; the repo has 12 hosts, including Xeon E5-1620 v4 and Core i5/i7/i3 desktop and laptop parts); Debian Jessie, kernel 4.4
stars_or_usage: 7.6k stars; the default BLAS of many Linux distributions, NumPy and Julia (usage not verified here)
tradeoffs: Hand-tuned assembly and intrinsics kernels per microarchitecture with DYNAMIC_ARCH runtime dispatch; provides BLAS, CBLAS and a LAPACK build, with extensions borrowed from MKL. Pthreads or OpenMP threading means thread-count and oversubscription tuning when embedded in another threaded program.
caveats: The win measured here is over the unoptimised Netlib reference BLAS and over single-threaded ATLAS, while OpenBLAS ran multi-threaded (thread count not stated), so the ratios mix threading with kernel quality. In the same data Intel MKL and multi-threaded ATLAS dev beat it on matrix multiply and eigenvalues (MKL 0.176 s vs OpenBLAS 0.500 s on the 640x640 eigenvalue test). The numbers are third-party: Andrzej Wojtowicz's blas-benchmarks (33 stars, Zenodo DOI, last update 2016-12-01) uses prebuilt Debian packages (OpenBLAS 0.2.12, which predates AVX-512 kernels and so most likely ran Haswell code on the Skylake Xeon), so compiler and flags are not stated and the tier stops at B. I read the figures from gen/data/benchmark.results.rds in that repo with a small script (the README has only bar-chart images) and took medians per test. The project's own docs make weaker, first-party claims: docs/faq.md says Sandy Bridge level 3 BLAS gave 'a performance comparable with Intel MKL' (single-thread DGEMM chart docs/dgemm_snb_1thread.png on a Core i5-2500K, no numbers in text) and that on the Loongson-3A it 'outperformed GotoBLAS by 135% in a single thread and 120% in 4 threads'. The lead URL xianyi/OpenBLAS now redirects to OpenMathLib/OpenBLAS.

name: PhysX
workload: Collision queries only: swept capsules cast downward onto a static terrain triangle mesh, 1 capsule and 100 capsules at random positions, time per query batch.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: 1 capsule 0.132 ms (PhysX) vs 0.757 ms (Bullet); 100 capsules 3.790 ms (PhysX) vs 73.388 ms (Bullet); the post summarises it as Bullet costing about 10 times more (ratios about 5.7x and 19.4x, derived from the snippet numbers).
stars_or_usage: 2.4k stars (PhysX-3.4 repo); widely embedded in game engines (usage not verified here)
tradeoffs: Full rigid-body, articulation, cloth and vehicle SDK with an optional NVIDIA-only CUDA GPU path; large code base. This repo is PhysX 3.4 with the deprecated APEX SDK; the README points cloth, destruction, particle and turbulence users to NvCloth, Blast, FleX and Flow.
caveats: Evidence is a WebSearch result snippet only (query: 'PhysX Bullet capsule sweep terrain 0.132ms 0.757ms 3.790ms 73.388ms'). The pages returned for it, cgpress.org 'physx performance versus bullet' and gamedev.net 'Efficiency : Bullet much slower than PhysX?', were EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the author, date, PhysX and Bullet versions, hardware, compiler and flags are unknown; the post is probably old and may not concern the 3.4 code in this repo. It measures sweep (raycast-style) queries on a mesh, not rigid-body stepping. It cannot be checked, so tier C at best, confidence low. I found no numeric PhysX comparison with ODE or Bullet in reachable pages: Pierre Terdiman's PEEL (https://github.com/Pierre-Terdiman/PEEL, 175 stars, the usual tool for PhysX against other engines) ships no results, the Gazebo benchmark (scpeters/benchmark) does not include PhysX, and the PhysX repo README has no performance text. Other searches returned only qualitative summaries, for example that Bullet beat PhysX for complex shapes in a haptic assembly study and that no engine wins every task. The lead's repo URL is the 2018 PhysX 3.4 snapshot; newer PhysX releases live elsewhere and were not opened.

name: Simbody
baseline: ODE and Bullet Physics, through Gazebo-classic's ODE and Bullet plugins (DART was measured in the same run)
workload: Real-time factor (wall-clock seconds per simulated second, lower is faster) in Gazebo-classic: free-floating 1x4x9 boxes, 1 to 101 boxes, with collision off and on; plus an object-stacking scene with a large inertia ratio.
claimed_speedup: No clear speed advantage over ODE or Bullet; Simbody is slower from 21 boxes up. Time ratio, 101 boxes (CSV): Simbody 1.84 (collision 0) and 1.87 (collision 1) vs ODE 1.58 and 1.34 vs Bullet 1.48 and 1.44, although Simbody ran with a 0.001 s step and ODE and Bullet with 0.0005 s; 1 box: Simbody 0.124 and 0.126 vs ODE 0.102 and 0.109 vs Bullet 0.127 and 0.129 (Simbody about 3% ahead of Bullet only there, and with half as many steps). ROSCon 2014 object-stacking slide, real/sim: ODE 0.4, Bullet 0.5, DART 1.1, Simbody >100. Simbody was faster than DART in the box test: 101 boxes 1.84 vs 4.37 (about 2.4x, derived from page data) and 1.87 vs 7.23 (about 3.9x, derived).
stars_or_usage: 2.6k stars; the physics engine behind OpenSim and an option in Gazebo
tradeoffs: Generalized (internal) coordinates with O(n) forward dynamics, so articulated chains have no constraint drift and implicit joint damping; it suits biomechanics and long chains rather than piles of free bodies. Contact is a compliant, force-based model with variable step size, which is slower for stiff stacking.
caveats: The README's only performance word is 'high-performance' (no numbers), and no benchmark in reachable pages shows Simbody faster than ODE or Bullet; this record documents that it was measured slower, so the orchestrator may want it as a REFERENCE or not-faster entry. The measurements come from the Gazebo maintainers' physics benchmark (https://github.com/scpeters/benchmark, slides https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scpeters/benchmark/HEAD/pdf/roscon2014_scpeters.pdf, ROSCon 2014), with results dated about 2014 to 2015, no CPU model, compiler or flags, and the engines running through Gazebo-classic wrappers, so Gazebo overhead is included. Simbody used a step twice as long as ODE and Bullet, so its cost per step is roughly double. The stacking slide's accuracy plot is not matched to speed. Simbody's strengths (O(n) multibody dynamics, accuracy for articulated systems) were not what this speed test targets; the Simbody paper and theory manual that may show such comparisons were not reachable.

name: SymEngine
workload: Ten symbolic workloads adapted from symengine's own C++ benchmark suite, run as SymEngine.jl v0.13.2 (libsymengine 0.12.0) against SymPy and SymbolicUtils.jl: derivative of expand((x^y+y^z+z^x)^50), 15-term series of sin(cos(1+x)), substitution into a random expression with 10^5 draws, variable search, numeric evaluation of a 10000-deep expression, lambda code generation and compiled-call time; minimum of samples, SymPy caches cleared before each sample.
claimed_speedup: SymEngine vs SymPy, seconds from the rendered table (ratios derived from page data): diff of expand((x^y+y^z+z^x)^50) 0.00696 vs 6.98 (about 1000x); series 15 terms 0.00199 vs 1.43 (about 720x); substitute trig product 1.48e-5 vs 6.57e-3 (about 440x); substitute 10^5-draw random expression, dense rule 0.00113 vs 2.30 (about 2000x) and sparse rule 0.00110 vs 1.07 (about 970x); variable search 0.00103 vs 0.0149 (about 15x) and on dissimilar expressions 0.000467 vs 0.00508 (about 11x); eval_double of a 10000-deep expression 0.0117 vs 31.06 (about 2660x); codegen init 0.00115 vs 0.0514 (about 45x); compiled call with CSE 6.93e-7 vs 8.41e-6 (about 12x).
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.13.0 (LLVM 20.1.8); libsymengine from SymEngine_jll v0.12.0+0 (a prebuilt binary, C++ compiler and flags not stated); SymPy from a conda environment (version not shown)
hardware: AMD EPYC 7502 32-Core Processor (128 virtual cores) on a SciML CI runner, Linux x86_64
stars_or_usage: 1.4k stars; backend of symengine.py, SymEngine.jl and others, optional core of SymPy and Sage (usage claim not verified here)
tradeoffs: Much smaller feature set than SymPy (no full simplify, solvers or integration); a C++ expression tree with reference-counted nodes, GMP or Boost integers, optional FLINT, MPFR, LLVM JIT and Piranha; usable from C, Python, Julia, Ruby, Haskell and others through wrappers.
caveats: The page is an independent benchmark (SciMLBenchmarks.jl, file benchmarks/Symbolics/SymEngineComparison.jmd, code public, CPU stated) but the workloads were adapted from SymEngine's own suite, so they favour a compiled symbolic kernel, and the same page's second set shows SymEngine losing to pure-Julia SymbolicUtils.jl on sparse-rule substitution (0.00110 s vs 0.000593 s), variable search (0.00103 s vs 0.00049 s) and the compiled call (6.93e-7 s vs 3.13e-7 s). SymEngine is reached through the SymEngine.jl wrapper (ccall) and SymPy through PythonCall, and the random expressions differ slightly between languages. Flags of the prebuilt libsymengine and the SymPy version are not on the page, hence B rather than A; the benchmark file was created in 2026, so it is a single recent run. SymEngine's repo has no README or wiki claim with SymPy numbers: the wiki pages found (Optimizing expand2b, Univariate Series expansion benchmarks) only compare SymEngine variants and Piranha (Piranha fateman1 13.4 ms vs SymEngine expand2d 14.3 ms, 2015). Older comparisons with GiNaC, Sage and CSymPy sit in blocked pages (Google Groups announcement, symengine.org, SciPy 2016 talk). The wave 8 categories have no symbolic-algebra bucket; big-integer-arbitrary-precision was chosen to sit beside FLINT and the orchestrator may override it. The lead's baseline was 'guess from the project's role'; SymPy is the one its description names.

name: sofia-ml
baseline: SVM-perf (SVM-perf-roc), SVM-light and SVM-struct-rank (Joachims' RankSVM solvers); for data parsing, Shalev-Shwartz's reference Pegasos and svm_perf
workload: Training a pairwise ranker equivalent to RankSVM by stochastic pairwise descent (100,000 stochastic steps): RCV1 E311 task with 781,265 training examples optimising ROC area, and LETOR 3.0 and 4.0 tasks of up to 70,000 examples; the README adds file read and parse speed.
claimed_speedup: RCV1 E311, CPU seconds for training at equal ROC area 0.9992: SPD Pegasos 0.20 s and SPD SGD-SVM 0.20 s (Passive-Aggressive 0.22 s, ROC area 0.9990) vs SVM-perf-roc 31.92 s (about 160x, derived from page data; the paper says more than 150x) and SVM-struct-rank 30,716.33 s. LETOR tasks: 0.2 to 0.3 CPU s per task, up to 100 times faster than SVM-light RankSVM and up to 5 times faster than SVM-struct-rank. README: reads and parses data nearly 10 times faster than the reference Pegasos implementation and nearly 3 times faster than svm_perf.
hardware: dual-core 2.8GHz laptop with 2G RAM (CPU model not stated)
stars_or_usage: 63 stars on this GitHub import (15 on rrenaud/sofia-ml); cited in learning-to-rank papers (not verified here)
tradeoffs: Approximate SGD solvers (Pegasos, SGD-SVM, passive-aggressive, margin perceptron, ROMMA, logistic regression) for linear models on sparse data; reaches the same ranking quality as exact RankSVM on the tested sets but gives no exact optimum or kernels. Command-line tool plus C++ API.
caveats: First-party numbers by the author (D. Sculley, Google) in the paper 'Large Scale Learning to Rank' that is checked into the repo; the PDF shows no venue, so I cannot confirm peer review. Hardware is a 2009-era laptop without a CPU model, and compiler and flags are not stated; the timing covers 100,000 SGD steps of an approximate learner against exact RankSVM solvers (SVM-light, SVM-struct-rank, SVM-perf-roc), so it measures an algorithm change, not just faster code. The RankSVM accuracy numbers are 'previously published' LETOR results rather than rerun. The 10x and 3x data-reading claims in the README give no method. Not compared with TensorFlow, PyTorch, liblinear or Vowpal Wabbit. The original code.google.com/p/sofia-ml page (the lead URL) was EGRESS_BLOCKED, so this record uses the GitHub import by glycerine (which GitHub shows as an export of the Google Code archive, last commit 2016-02-13; its earliest commits date from December 2009).
